subtype: Caring for a sick loved one [Response]
passage:
Friday night
Amma's fever has been up and down since Wednesday. I've kept a jug of water and some coconut water by her bed and reminded her to sip every time I pass. She snapped at me twice today: once for opening the curtains, once for asking if she'd eaten. Old me would have sulked. Today I just said, 'Okay, Amma,' and closed them. That's the fever talking, not her. This evening she seemed confused about what day it was, and that frightened me. I called Dr Nirmala's clinic straight away. She said to bring Amma in tonight, so Ravi Mama is driving us now. Writing this in the car.
Aadhya

qa.q: Who is driving them to the clinic?
qa.a: Ravi Mama.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when Amma seemed confused about the day?
qa.a: Aadhya felt frightened and worried, and acted straight away.

qa.q: Which of Aadhya's actions show wise caregiving?
qa.a: Keeping fluids near, letting Amma rest, not taking the snapping personally, and calling the doctor when a worrying sign appeared.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Aadhya closed the curtains without arguing?
qa.a: Amma probably felt relieved and understood, too ill to explain why the light bothered her.

grounding: A caregiver keeps fluids and rest in view, accepts a sick parent's grumpiness and calls the doctor at a worrying sign.

passage:
School nurse's note, Class 5, Monday
Avni came to the sick room at lunch saying she had a stomach ache, but mostly she wanted to hide. Her class teacher says she has started wearing her sweater all day in the heat and snaps at friends who tease her for growing taller than the boys. When I asked gently, she whispered that her chest is changing, she hates it, and her body feels like it belongs to someone else. I told her plainly that bodies start changing at different times, that it is normal and nothing to be ashamed of, and showed her a simple picture book about growing up. With her permission, I phoned her mother this afternoon so they can talk at home and shop for a comfortable vest together.
Jaya

qa.q: What did Avni say she had when she came to the sick room?
qa.a: A stomach ache.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about her changing body?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and self-conscious, as if her body belongs to someone else.

qa.q: What did Jaya do that reduced Avni's shame?
qa.a: Jaya explained plainly that bodies change at different times and that it's normal, showed a simple picture book, and with permission called her mother.

qa.q: How might the friends who tease see Avni's sweater?
qa.a: They may think it's strange or funny, not knowing Avni is trying to hide changes that feel embarrassing.

grounding: A child beginning puberty feels embarrassed and moody, and an honest, simple explanation from an adult reduces her shame.

passage: Madhuri was leaving at dawn for a three-day school camp, and the bag was still half packed when she came home giggling. 'Ma, Sneha says girls bleed and it hurts like a knife and you can't swim ever again!' Parveen's first instinct was to laugh it off; there was no time tonight. Then the power went out. In the candlelight, folding clothes, Parveen talked plainly and without hurry: that periods come to most girls some time in these years, that it's a normal part of growing up, how pads work, and that the teachers at camp would help. She tucked two pads and spare underwear into a side pocket. 'Just in case. Nothing to be scared of.' Madhuri nodded, curious now, not frightened.

qa.q: What did Parveen tuck into the side pocket?
qa.a: Two pads and spare underwear.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel after the candlelit talk?
qa.a: She felt curious and calm, no longer frightened by the rumours.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Parveen to talk despite the rush?
qa.a: Plain, unhurried facts before camp replaced Sneha's scary rumours and gave Madhuri confidence and a plan.

qa.q: What would change if Parveen had laughed it off?
qa.a: Madhuri would go to camp with only rumours and fear, and might feel alone if her period started there.

grounding: A parent explains periods plainly before they happen, replacing rumour and fear with confidence.

passage: At the boys' hostel of the residential school, Vishal's day swung like a pendulum. At breakfast he laughed so hard at Arnab's impression of the maths teacher that milk came out of his nose. By lunch, after a short 'no' from a girl he liked about going to the fest together, he lay face-down on his bunk, sure everything was ruined. At evening games he shouted at a junior over a missed catch, then sat alone on the steps, shaking. Arnab sat beside him. 'Bro, this morning you were the happiest guy alive.' 'I know,' Vishal muttered. 'It feels huge. Then it doesn't. I can't keep up with myself.' Arnab didn't laugh. He stayed till the dinner bell.

qa.q: What made Vishal laugh at breakfast?
qa.a: Arnab's impression of the maths teacher.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel lying face-down on his bunk?
qa.a: He felt crushed and hopeless over one small 'no', sure everything was ruined.

qa.q: How did Arnab support Vishal?
qa.a: He took the feelings seriously, didn't laugh, and simply stayed with him till the dinner bell.

qa.q: How might the junior have felt when Vishal shouted?
qa.a: The junior probably felt scared and hurt over one missed catch.

grounding: A teenager's feelings swing from delight to despair in a day, and the intensity is real even when the trigger is small.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Sarika walked three steps ahead of her father and rolled her eyes when Pankaj waved at her friends. In the classroom she answered her teacher in full sentences but gave him only shrugs. On the way out, Pankaj stood by the notice board, stung. 'At home too,' he said quietly to the class teacher. 'Door shut, earphones in. She used to tell me everything.' The teacher smiled. 'She's kind in class and working hard. Pulling away from parents at this age is usually normal. Just stay easy to find.' That evening Pankaj left a cup of hot chocolate outside her door with a note: 'No questions. Here if you want to talk.' An hour later she came out and sat beside him watching cricket, saying nothing. It was enough.

qa.q: What did Pankaj leave outside Sarika's door?
qa.a: A cup of hot chocolate with a note.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel by the notice board?
qa.a: He felt stung and rejected, missing the daughter who used to tell him everything.

qa.q: What did the class teacher advise, and how did Pankaj use it?
qa.a: To stay easy to find without pressure; Pankaj left a no-questions note offering to talk.

qa.q: What might Sarika have felt about her father waving at her friends?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and wanted some independence, which does not mean she stopped loving him.

grounding: A father hurt by his teenage daughter's sudden distance learns it is normal and stays available without pressure.

passage:
'Ammi, everyone in my class looks older than me. Zoya already looks like a college student. I still look like a little kid.'
'Who said that?'
'Nobody. Everyone. At the swimming lesson the others laughed that I look ten.'
Farida put down the knife. 'Dilnaz, come here. I was the shortest in my class till I was fifteen. Then I shot up in one year.'
'Really?'
'Really. Bodies have their own clocks. Early, late, both are normal. And none of it measures what you're worth.'
'But I feel like a baby next to them.'
'I know it feels awkward. Shall I talk to your coach about the teasing?'
'No... maybe. Yes.'
Dilnaz leaned against her mother's shoulder, a little lighter.

qa.q: Where did the others laugh at Dilnaz?
qa.a: At the swimming lesson.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz feel next to classmates?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels awkward and left behind, like a baby next to them, and hurt by the laughing.

qa.q: What reassurance did Farida give?
qa.a: That bodies have their own clocks, early or late are both normal, and none of it measures worth; she also offered to talk to the coach.

qa.q: How might Farida feel hearing about the teasing?
qa.a: Farida probably feels protective and sympathetic, remembering being the shortest in her own class.

grounding: A teenager maturing later than classmates feels awkward and teased, and a parent reassures her that timing varies and worth is not measured by body.

passage: Last year Salma was the loudest voice in my Class 9 English period, always first to volunteer. Around February she changed. She sat at the back, flinched at a harmless joke about her handwriting and spent breaks alone in the library. At first I told myself it was teenage moods, so I gave her space and didn't call on her in class. But after three weeks, when she wrote in an essay that 'nothing feels worth trying anymore,' I knew space wasn't enough. I asked her to stay back, just to chat. 'Sangeeta Ma'am, I'm fine,' she said, eyes down. I told her I was glad she was in my class and that I'd noticed she seemed sad. That same afternoon, with the school counsellor, I called her mother. Salma now meets the counsellor every week.

qa.q: Where did Salma spend breaks after February?
qa.a: Alone in the library.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta feel that space wasn't enough?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt worried when Salma wrote that nothing felt worth trying anymore, after weeks of withdrawal.

qa.q: What steps did Sangeeta take?
qa.a: She gently told Salma she'd noticed the sadness, and that same afternoon called Salma's mother together with the school counsellor.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt when Sangeeta Ma'am said she was glad Salma was in the class?
qa.a: Salma may have felt seen and a little relieved, even while saying she was fine.

grounding: A teacher notices a cheerful student turn withdrawn and, when sadness lasts, involves the family and a counsellor the same day.

passage: Ayesha, promise you won't laugh. Okay. So Leela, the girl who said crushes are silly, has a crush. On Rehaan from debate club. Whenever he walks past, my face goes hot, my stomach flips and I forget how to talk. Last week I went red just because he borrowed my pen. It's so confusing. My body does things I didn't ask for, and I kept thinking something was wrong with me, or that Mummy would be furious. Then an older boy from tuition started messaging me to meet him secretly, and I almost said yes just to feel grown-up. Instead I told my Masi that same evening. She didn't scold. She said these feelings are normal, that I get to go slow, and that anyone who wants secrets from adults isn't safe. I blocked that boy that night. Rehaan can stay a nice feeling for now.

qa.q: What happens when Rehaan walks past Leela?
qa.a: Her face goes hot, her stomach flips, and she forgets how to talk.

qa.q: What was Leela worried about?
qa.a: She was anxious that something was wrong with her and scared that Mummy would be furious.

qa.q: What did Masi help Leela decide?
qa.a: That the feelings are normal, she can go slow, and anyone wanting secrets from adults isn't safe, so Leela blocked the older boy.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel hearing Leela's story?
qa.a: Ayesha may feel trusted, and relieved that Leela talked to Masi instead of meeting the older boy.

grounding: A teenager with a first crush and confusing feelings turns to a trusted adult and chooses care over secrecy.

passage:
Counsellor's follow-up note, Karthik, Class 11
Two months ago Karthik came to me after smashing his phone against a wall over a group-chat fight and sending messages he deeply regretted. Today was very different. He told me that on Saturday a friend posted something hurtful about him. He felt the heat rise and typed a furious reply, then remembered our plan: wait an hour before sending anything. He went for a run round the colony instead, then played his guitar. When the hour was up, he deleted the draft, and he called the friend the next day to talk calmly. He said, 'The feeling was huge, but it passed.' I told him I was proud of him. We will meet monthly now.
Parveen

qa.q: What did Karthik do instead of sending the reply?
qa.a: He went for a run round the colony, then played his guitar.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when the friend posted something hurtful?
qa.a: He felt a rush of anger, with heat rising, and typed a furious reply.

qa.q: Which strategy helped Karthik, and why?
qa.a: Waiting an hour before sending anything, with a run and music as outlets, let the big feeling pass so he could talk calmly.

qa.q: How might the friend have experienced Karthik's calm call?
qa.a: The friend may have felt relieved and more willing to talk than if a furious message had arrived.

grounding: A teenager learns that big feelings pass, uses running and music as outlets, and waits before sending a message.

subtopic: Menstrual cycle effects on mood and coping
subtype: First period and feelings about it [Actor]
passage:
Wednesday
It happened. In the middle of social studies I felt something strange, and in the girls' toilet I saw the stain. My heart was thumping. I didn't know whether to cry or laugh. Aadhya noticed my face and handed me the spare pad from her bag without a single question. Best friend ever. I tied my sweater round my waist for the rest of the day.
At home I told Ammi. I was so nervous, but she hugged me and said, 'My girl is growing up.' She made me hot haldi milk and showed me where she keeps supplies in the cupboard, and explained what to expect each month, plainly, like it was ordinary. It kind of is. I feel embarrassed, proud and a bit grown-up all at once.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Aadhya hand Sabina?
qa.a: The spare pad from her bag.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel about her first period?
qa.a: She felt nervous at first, then embarrassed, proud and a bit grown-up all at once.

qa.q: What made the day easier for Sabina?
qa.a: Aadhya's quiet help and Ammi's calm hug, supplies and plain explanation, which made it feel ordinary.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have felt seeing Sabina's face?
qa.a: Aadhya probably felt caring and understanding, helping quickly without questions to spare Sabina embarrassment.

grounding: A girl with her first period feels nervous, proud and embarrassed at once, and supplies and a calm adult make it ordinary.
